blocks.text: Rate limiting controls how many requests or operations are allowed within a period of time.
Limits can apply per user, API key, IP address, or service. They help control load, abuse, and usage costs.
An API allows each API key to make 100 requests per minute. Requests above that limit are rejected.
HTTP APIs commonly return status 429 (Too Many Requests). A Retry-After header can tell the client how long to wait.
A fixed window counts requests in each time interval. Requests near a window boundary can create a burst.
A sliding window considers recent traffic as time moves forward.
A token bucket adds tokens at a steady rate. Each request consumes a token, allowing short bursts up to the bucket capacity.
A limit enforced separately on each server can allow more total traffic as servers are added. A shared limit needs coordination.
Rate limiting caps arrivals over time. Bulkheads cap resource use or concurrent work, while circuit breakers react to dependency failures.
